html:
On St. George's Night, 23 April 1343, Estonian peasants in the north rose against their German and Danish lords, burning manors and the monastery at Padise. It was the largest revolt of the native people of medieval Livonia.

The rebels killed many Germans and besieged Tallinn, and they asked Sweden for help. But the Livonian Order invited their leaders to talks and killed them, then crushed the rebel armies. The fighting went on in the islands until 1345.

Shaken, the Danish king sold northern Estonia to the Teutonic Order in 1346. German landlords ruled the countryside for centuries, and Estonians lived as serfs. In the 1800s the uprising became a symbol of resistance for the national movement, before the War of Independence.
